question: EPS is calculated as:
before: EPS uses Net Profit (PAT) -- the profit attributable to equity shareholders. Revenue, EBITDA, or Gross Profit do not represent actual earnings available to shareholders.
after:
Formula: EPS = Net Profit (PAT) / Outstanding Shares, where Net Profit (PAT) is profit after tax (the bottom line of the income statement), and Outstanding Shares is the total number of equity shares issued and held by shareholders.

Step-by-step: EPS measures the earnings attributable to each equity share. To calculate it, you take the total profit available to equity shareholders (Net Profit or PAT) and divide it by the number of shares outstanding. This gives the rupee earnings per individual share.

Why this is correct: Net Profit (PAT) is the only metric that represents actual profit left after all expenses, interest, taxes, and other charges have been deducted. Only this bottom-line profit belongs to equity shareholders, so dividing it by shares outstanding gives the true earning power per share that investors care about.

Why the others are wrong: Option A (Revenue / Shares) — Revenue is the top line and includes no cost deductions; it does not represent profit available to shareholders. Option B (EBITDA / Shares) — EBITDA excludes interest and taxes, which are real cash outflows owed before equity holders receive anything; it is not shareholders' profit. Option D (Gross Profit / Shares) — Gross Profit only deducts cost of goods sold and ignores operating expenses, interest, and taxes; it is far too high and does not reflect actual profit to shareholders.

Intuition: EPS is the fundamental metric that tells an equity analyst how much profit each share is generating. Only the profit that survives all obligations (taxes, debt, operating costs) matters to shareholders; revenue and intermediate profit figures mislead because they include money that will never reach equity holders.
